title: Git & Workflows
description: Commits, PRs, parallel worktrees and test-driven loops with Claude.

lessons.title: Commits & PRs
lessons.description: Let Claude handle the git chores

theory.title: Git in plain words
theory.body:
**Git** records the history of your project.

A **diff** is the list of lines added or removed since the last save. A **commit** is a saved snapshot of your changes, with a message saying what changed and why.

Before committing, you **stage** changes (`git add`): staging picks which edits go into the next commit.

A **branch** is a separate line of work. `main` is the shared one, so new work usually happens on its own branch. A **pull request (PR)** asks teammates to review your branch and merge it into `main`.
theory.code:
git diff            # changes NOT yet staged
git diff --staged   # changes staged for the next commit
                    # (--cached means the same thing)
git log --oneline   # commit history, one line each
gh pr create        # open a pull request (GitHub CLI)

theory.title: Claude speaks git
theory.body:
You don't need to remember git commands to use them with Claude. Ask in plain words, like the prompts below. Ask for a commit message that explains **why** the change was made, not just what changed.

For PRs, Claude uses the GitHub CLI, `gh`. Install it and run `gh auth login` once so it can act on your GitHub account.

Kip tip: Claude links the session to the PR it creates, so `claude --from-pr 123` finds that conversation later.
theory.code:
> review the staged diff for bugs and missing tests
> commit with a message explaining why the change was made
> create a pr

theory.title: Review the diff before it ships
theory.body:
Claude's edits can look plausible and still be wrong. The diff is the ground truth of what changed, so read it yourself with `git diff --staged`, or ask Claude to **review the diff for bugs, edge cases and missing tests**.

Keep work off `main`: ask for a new branch with a clear name like `fix/cart-total`. After Claude writes a PR, ask it to highlight risks you should double-check.

exercises.prompt: Which tool does Claude use to open GitHub pull requests from your terminal?
exercises.explanation: Git itself knows nothing about pull requests, so Claude needs GitHub's own CLI, `gh`, installed and logged in.

exercises.prompt: Why review the diff before letting Claude commit?
options: Git refuses commits without a review
Claude can't write commit messages without it
Edits can look plausible but be wrong; the diff shows exactly what changed
exercises.explanation: The diff is the ground truth of what changed, so it's where you catch subtle mistakes before they enter history.

exercises.prompt: Claude opened PR #1234 last week. How do you jump back to that session?
exercises.explanation: Claude links each session to the PR it created, so `claude --from-pr` can find that conversation by PR number.

exercises.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
exercises.explanation: Inspect with diff, check history with log, and ship with gh: knowing which is which lets you verify what Claude did.

exercises.prompt: Claude just fixed a cart total bug and you want it shipped for review.
options: Create a branch fix/cart-total, commit the fix with a message explaining the bug, and open a PR against main describing the change and how you tested it.
exercises.explanation: Pushing to main skips review entirely, while a branch plus a PR lets teammates check the change before it lands.

exercises.code:
> review the ___ diff for bugs and missing tests
> commit with a message explaining ___ the change was made
> create a ___
exercises.hint: Review what will be committed, ask for the reason behind it, then open a pull request.
exercises.explanation: The staged diff is exactly what the commit will contain, and a message that explains why helps future readers more than one that lists what.

exercises.prompt: Order a careful ship-it flow with Claude.
steps: Ask Claude to summarize the changes you made
Ask Claude to review the diff for bugs and missing tests
Ask Claude to commit with a descriptive message
Ask Claude to create a pr
Read the PR and ask Claude to flag any risks
exercises.explanation: Problems are cheapest to fix before the commit, so you summarize and review first and only then commit and open the PR.

exercises.prompt: In your shell, show the changes that are staged for the next commit.
exercises.explanation: Plain `git diff` hides staged changes, so you add `--staged` to see exactly what the next commit will contain.

exercises.scenario: Claude just fixed a timezone bug in the date parser and added tests. Write one prompt that gets the change reviewed, committed and opened as a PR.
exercises.sample: Context: you just fixed the timezone bug in @src/utils/date.ts and added tests in @tests/date.test.ts. Goal: get this reviewed and opened as a PR. First review the diff for bugs or missing edge cases, then run the tests. Constraints: don't commit to main; use a new branch fix/date-timezone. If the tests pass, commit with a message explaining the timezone bug and create a pr that describes the fix and how it was tested. Done when the PR is open and you reply with its link and any risks I should double-check.
exercises.explanation: A strong ship prompt chains review, verification, commit and PR in order, so nothing reaches reviewers untested.

theory.title: Worktrees in plain words
theory.body:
Normally your project folder shows one branch at a time. A **git worktree** is an **extra folder** showing a different branch of the same repo. Files are separate; history (commits) is shared.

Run one Claude session per worktree and they can't overwrite each other's edits. Kip runs three at once and never pinches his own claw.

In `git worktree add ../project-feature-a -b feature-a`: `add` creates a worktree, `../project-feature-a` is the new folder's path (`..` puts it next to your project), and `-b feature-a` creates a new branch with that name.

`&&` joins two commands: run the second only if the first worked. The repo needs at least one commit first.
theory.code:
# new folder ../project-feature-a on new branch feature-a
git worktree add ../project-feature-a -b feature-a

# go there, then start Claude
cd ../project-feature-a && claude

git worktree list                          # every worktree + its branch
git worktree remove ../project-feature-a   # clean up when done

theory.title: Let Claude Code make it
theory.body:
Shortcut: `claude --worktree <name>` (short `-w`) creates a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` and starts Claude inside it, all in one command.

When the work is finished: review it, commit it, and merge its branch (usually through a PR). Then remove the worktree so old folders don't pile up.
theory.code:
claude --worktree feature-auth
# same thing
claude -w feature-auth

theory.title: The test-driven loop
theory.body:
A **test** is a small piece of code that checks your code gives the expected output. It **passes** (green) or **fails** (red). TDD means writing tests first. They give Claude a clear target it can check itself.

**1.** Ask Claude to write tests from concrete examples, and say you're doing TDD so it doesn't write the implementation yet.

**2.** Run them and confirm they **fail**. A test that already passes isn't checking anything new. Commit the tests.

**3.** Ask Claude to write code that makes them pass **without modifying the tests**, iterating until green.

**4.** Commit the code.
theory.code:
> we're doing TDD. write tests for slugify():
  'Hello World' -> 'hello-world'. no implementation yet
> run the tests and confirm they fail, then commit them
> implement slugify until the tests pass. don't modify the tests

exercises.prompt: Why use worktrees for parallel Claude sessions?
options: Each has independent files but shared history, so sessions don't overwrite each other
They let two sessions share one context window
exercises.explanation: Two sessions editing one folder would clobber each other's files, while separate worktrees keep files apart and commits in one repo.

exercises.prompt: Mid-loop, Claude suggests changing a test's expected value so it passes. What should you usually do?
options: Tell Claude to keep the tests unchanged and fix the implementation
exercises.explanation: The tests encode what the code should do, so editing them to pass hides the bug instead of fixing it.

exercises.prompt: You want to build slugify() test-first.
options: Write tests in tests/slugify.test.ts for slugify(): 'Hello World' -> 'hello-world', '  Trim me  ' -> 'trim-me', '' -> ''. We're doing TDD, so don't write the implementation yet. Run the tests and confirm they fail.
Write slugify and some tests for it.
exercises.explanation: Concrete input/output pairs define the target, and 'no implementation yet' stops Claude writing tests that just match its own code.

exercises.code:
git worktree ___ ../app-bugfix -b bugfix
cd ../app-bugfix && claude
git worktree ___
git worktree ___ ../app-bugfix
exercises.hint: git worktree add <path> -b <branch>, then list, then remove <path>.
exercises.explanation: A worktree's life is create, use, check, clean up, and each step is a git worktree subcommand: add, list, remove.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to run a parallel Claude session in a worktree.
steps: Run claude and give it the feature task
Review, commit and merge the feature-a branch
exercises.explanation: The folder must exist before you can work in it, and you remove it only after its branch is merged so no work is lost.

exercises.prompt: Order the test-driven loop with Claude.
steps: Ask Claude to write tests from expected inputs and outputs, no implementation
Run the tests and confirm they fail
Ask Claude to write code that passes without changing the tests
Iterate until green, then commit the code
exercises.explanation: Seeing the tests fail first proves they check something, and committing them locks the target before any code is written.

exercises.prompt: Create a worktree in the folder ../project-feature-a on a new branch named feature-a.
exercises.explanation: `-b` creates a fresh branch for the new folder, so its work stays separate from the branch you're on.

exercises.prompt: Start Claude in an isolated worktree named feature-auth, letting Claude Code create the worktree for you.
exercises.explanation: `--worktree` creates the folder and starts Claude in it in one step, so you skip the manual add and cd.

exercises.prompt: List all worktrees for this repository.
exercises.hint: git worktree <subcommand>: the one that lists.
exercises.explanation: With several parallel sessions it's easy to lose track, and `git worktree list` shows every folder and its branch.

exercises.scenario: You need parseDuration("1h30m") to return 5400 (seconds). Kick off a TDD loop with Claude.
exercises.sample: Context: we need parseDuration in @src/time.ts to turn strings like "1h30m" into seconds, and we're doing TDD. Goal: write tests in @tests/time.test.ts first: "1h30m" -> 5400, "45s" -> 45, "2h" -> 7200, and invalid input throws. Constraints: don't write the implementation yet. Run the tests, confirm they fail, and commit them. Then implement parseDuration without modifying the tests. Done when every test passes and the implementation is committed separately from the tests.
exercises.explanation: Concrete examples, a tests-first rule and a 'don't modify tests' constraint give Claude a target it can't quietly move.

mission.title: Ship It From a Worktree
mission.intro: Spin up a parallel workspace, drive a tiny feature test-first, and ship it as a real PR.
checklist: Create a worktree: claude --worktree tiny-feature (or git worktree add ../repo-tiny -b tiny-feature)
Ask Claude to write failing tests for a small function, run them, and commit the tests
Have Claude implement the function until the tests pass without touching the tests
Ask Claude to review the git diff, then commit with a descriptive message
With gh installed and logged in, ask Claude to create a pr
mission.explanation: Worktree isolation, a TDD loop and a reviewed PR are the core of a safe Claude git workflow.

cheatsheet.description: Ask Claude to open a pull request via the gh CLI.
Authenticate the GitHub CLI so Claude can create PRs.
Show staged changes; review before committing.
Find sessions linked to a pull request.
Create a separate checkout on a new branch.
Start Claude in a new isolated worktree (short: -w).
Show all worktrees and their branches.
Delete a worktree when you're done.
Write failing tests, commit them, implement until green without editing tests.
